MORCIC aims to reduce electromagnetic RLCk models of integrated circuits to smaller ROMs with similar accuracy to commercial tools.
The proposed MOR techniques achieve up to 5.5 times smaller ROMs compared to ANSYS RaptorX™.
RLCk models can have over 1 million elements and more than 10 ports, posing challenges for reduction.
Moment Matching methods are computationally efficient but depend on ad-hoc moment selection and struggle with multi-port models.
Balanced Truncation provides reliable error bounds and handles multi-port models but is computationally expensive for large-scale systems.
MORCIC uses low-rank approximations and Extended Krylov Subspace methods to solve Lyapunov equations efficiently.
The state-space form of an RLCk circuit involves matrices G, C, B, and L representing conductance, capacitance, input, and output connectivity.
The output error in the frequency domain is bounded by the difference in transfer functions' H-infinity norm.
Initial BT MOR was tested on small-scale models with up to 21,800 nodes and achieved reduction percentages of 65-87%.
Mean relative error (MRE) and maximum relative error (MAX RE) for DC and SP analyses were below 0.73% and 1.89%, respectively, in initial BT tests.
Low-rank BT MOR was validated on large-scale RLCk models extracted in 22nm FDSOI technology.
Benchmark circuits included Hybrid and Wilkinson couplers, VGAs, VCOs, and LNAs with initial orders up to 162,881 and millions of mutual inductors.
MORCIC ROMs showed insertion loss errors below 0.5 dB and phase differences less than 2 degrees compared to RaptorX™ ROMs.
MORCIC's reduction time and memory usage are higher than RaptorX™ but remain reasonable and subject to future optimization.
The MORCIC tool is implemented in C++ with CMake and runs on Linux workstations with multi-threaded Intel Xeon CPUs and 64 GB RAM.
Balanced Truncation involves computing controllability and observability Gramians by solving Lyapunov equations.
Low-rank BT projects Lyapunov equations onto Krylov subspaces to reduce computational complexity from O(N^3) to O(k^3), with k << N.
The MORCIC project received funding from the European Regional Development Fund and Greek national funds.
ANSYS RaptorX™ is a commercial tool used as a benchmark for comparison in this research.
The MORCIC approach can be integrated into industrial extraction tools to improve model compactness and simulation speed.
